title.en: typing.Protocol: Structural Typing and Duck Typing Written Down

description.en: Describe the behaviour a function needs with a Protocol instead of a base class. Learn what @runtime_checkable really checks, and why signatures are the type checker's job.

story_variants.en:
## Typing by Behaviour, Not by Family Tree

"Think of a power socket," Vaathiyaar says. "It does not care who made the plug. It only cares that the pins fit. Python's duck typing works that way, and `typing.Protocol` lets you *write the socket down* so that tools and readers can see it."

### A protocol is a list of required behaviour

```
from typing import Protocol

class Closeable(Protocol):
    def close(self) -> None: ...
```

Any class that has a `close()` method fits `Closeable`. It does **not** inherit from it or register with it. This is called *structural* typing, in contrast to *nominal* typing (a class is a `Closeable` only if it says so).

### Checking at run time

A static checker such as mypy uses protocols without any extra code. For `isinstance` you must opt in:

```
from typing import runtime_checkable

@runtime_checkable
class Closeable(Protocol):
    def close(self) -> None: ...

isinstance(open_file, Closeable)    # True
```

> **Vaathiyaar's honest caveat:** a runtime check only looks at whether the **attribute exists**. It does not check argument lists or return types. A class whose `close` needs three arguments still passes `isinstance`. Static checkers are the tool that compares signatures.

Today you define a `Scorer` protocol and write `best()`, which picks the highest-scoring candidate and ignores objects that do not fit.

explanation.en: List the members; the body is just ...
Opt in so isinstance can test the shape
True when the attribute exists, whatever the class's ancestry

instruction.en: Define a `@runtime_checkable` `Scorer` protocol with a `score(self, text: str) -> float` method, then implement `best(candidates, text)`: keep only the candidates that are a `Scorer`, and return the class name (`type(x).__name__`) of the one whose `score(text)` is highest. Then print `best([Rogue(), VowelScorer(), LengthScorer()], "protocols")` (expected: `LengthScorer`, because 9 beats 3 vowels).

en: Put `@runtime_checkable` on the line above `class Scorer(Protocol):`.
Filter with `isinstance(c, Scorer)`; `Rogue` has no `score`, so it drops out.

q.en: Does a class need to inherit from a Protocol to satisfy it?
q.ta: ஒரு class ஒரு Protocol-ஐப் பூர்த்தி செய்ய அதிலிருந்து inherit செய்ய வேண்டுமா?

en: No, having the required members is enough
Only if the Protocol has attributes
Only if it is decorated with @dataclass

q.en: What happens with `isinstance(x, SomeProtocol)` when the protocol is not decorated with @runtime_checkable?
A class has `def close(self, a, b, c)`. The protocol says `def close(self) -> None`. What does `isinstance(obj, Closeable)` return at run time?
q.ta: ஒரு class-இல் `def close(self, a, b, c)` உள்ளது. Protocol `def close(self) -> None` என்கிறது. run time-இல் `isinstance(obj, Closeable)` என்ன தரும்?

en: False, because the argument lists differ
True, because the runtime check only looks for the attribute
ta: True, ஏனெனில் run time சோதனை attribute இருக்கிறதா என்று மட்டுமே பார்க்கும்

q.en: Which tool is responsible for noticing the wrong signature in the previous question?
q.ta: முந்தைய கேள்வியில் தவறான signature-ஐக் கண்டறிவது எந்தக் கருவி?

en: The Python interpreter, when the module is imported
A static type checker such as mypy or pyright
ta: mypy அல்லது pyright போன்ற static type checker

under_the_hood.summary: A Protocol names the members a type must have. Type checkers compare names and signatures statically; runtime_checkable lets isinstance test only that the attributes exist.

steps.title: Nominal and structural typing
steps.body: With nominal typing a class is a `Closeable` only if it inherits from `Closeable`. With structural typing it is one if it has the right members. Python's duck typing was always structural, but only implicit: nothing in the code said what a function expected. A `Protocol` writes that expectation down.

left.label: Nominal (inheritance)

right.label: Structural (Protocol)

steps.title: What a Protocol class contains
steps.body: A protocol body lists members with bodies of `...`. The class is never meant to be instantiated; calling `Closeable()` raises `TypeError`. Its job is to be read by type checkers, and (if marked) by `isinstance`. Protocols can also declare attributes, such as `name: str`.

steps.title: The static check compares signatures
steps.body: A tool such as mypy or pyright checks that `close` exists, that its parameters accept the call the protocol describes, and that the return type is compatible. Python itself does none of this when running your program; type hints are ignored at run time. So a wrong signature is reported by the checker, not by the interpreter.

stages.label: Pass an object to a function that expects it

steps.title: What runtime_checkable adds
steps.body: `@runtime_checkable` lets `isinstance(obj, Closeable)` work. Python then checks only that every protocol member exists as an attribute on `obj`, using `hasattr`-style lookups. Without the decorator, `isinstance` against a protocol raises `TypeError`. That is why a class with `close(self, a, b, c)` still passes the check.

stepDescriptions.description: The decorator turns on isinstance support for this protocol.
Conn has an attribute named close, so the check passes. Its signature is not examined.
Note has no close attribute, so the check fails.

steps.title: When to reach for a Protocol
steps.body: Use one when you accept many unrelated types that share a behaviour (files, sockets, your own classes) and you do not control their base classes. Prefer an abstract base class when you want shared code or a registry of subclasses. Keep protocols small, one or two methods, so more types fit them.

under_the_hood.takeaway: Protocols describe the shape you need instead of the family tree. Rely on a type checker for signatures; treat a runtime isinstance check as a presence test only.
